title: ps, top, systemctl and journalctl in practice
summary: The commands that answer 'what is running', 'why is it slow' and 'why did it fail to start' — with the output details that matter.

sections.heading: ps: precise, scriptable
sections.html:
# top CPU consumers with parent and userps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,pcpu,pmem,etime,cmd --sort=-pcpu | head -12
# full command line for one processps -fp 4242
# process tree (see who spawned what)ps -ef --forest | less
# threads of a processps -T -p 4242
# find by namepgrep -a nginx

Reading the columns: STAT is the state (see the previous lesson), etime is elapsed time since start (useful to spot a process that restarted recently), pcpu is average CPU over the process's lifetime — not instantaneous, which is why a process that spiked and settled can look calm in ps but hot in top.

sections.heading: top and htop: live view
sections.html:
Useful keys in top: P sort by CPU, M sort by memory, H show threads, 1 per-CPU breakdown, c full command line, k kill (avoid — use kill deliberately).

Read the header before the process list:

top - 12:04:11 up 3 days,  2:11,  2 users,  load average: 4.12, 3.80, 2.95
Tasks: 214 total,   2 running, 211 sleeping,   0 stopped,   1 zombie
%Cpu(s): 62.3 us,  4.1 sy,  0.0 ni, 30.1 id,  3.2 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.3 si
MiB Mem :   7862.0 total,    412.3 free,   5210.4 used,   2239.3 buff/cache
MiB Swap:   2048.0 total,   2048.0 free,      0.0 used
  • load average counts runnable and uninterruptible tasks. Compare with core count: 4.12 on 4 cores is saturated; on 16 cores it is fine.
  • wa (iowait) high means processes are waiting on storage — renicing will not help.
  • sy (system) high suggests syscall or context-switch overhead, often networking or many small IO operations.
  • buff/cache is not 'used' in the problematic sense; Linux uses free memory for cache and reclaims it on demand.
  • 1 zombie is usually harmless; hundreds indicate a parent that never reaps.

sections.heading: systemd: services versus processes
sections.html:
A process is a running program. A service (unit) is a managed resource with a lifecycle, dependencies, restart policy, resource limits and logging. systemd is PID 1: it starts units, tracks them, restarts them on failure and collects their output into the journal.

# state, exit code and recent log lines in one viewsystemctl status myapp.service
# is it enabled at boot? is it active now?systemctl is-enabled myapp; systemctl is-active myapp
# what does the unit actually run?systemctl cat myapp.service
# effective settings after drop-inssystemctl show -p User,Group,ExecStart,Restart,TimeoutStopSec myapp
# lifecyclesudo systemctl restart myapp
sudo systemctl reload myapp      # only if the unit defines ExecReload
# why did it fail?journalctl -u myapp -n 80 --no-pager
journalctl -u myapp --since '10 min ago' -p err

The distinction that matters in an interview: systemctl restart asks systemd to stop and start the unit, applying the unit's stop signal and timeout. kill acts on a process and bypasses all of that — including any restart policy, which may then immediately restart it and confuse you.

sections.heading: journalctl: reading logs properly
sections.html:
# this boot, errors onlyjournalctl -b -p err --no-pager
# follow a unit livejournalctl -u myapp -f
# time-bounded (incident window)journalctl --since '2026-11-17 09:00' --until '2026-11-17 09:30'
# kernel messages (interface flaps, OOM killer)journalctl -k -b | tail -40
# disk usage of the journal itselfjournalctl --disk-usage

Two things to look for specifically: the OOM killer (Out of memory: Killed process 4242 (java)) which explains a service that 'randomly died', and interface events (eth0: link is not ready) which explain network blips. Both live in the kernel log, not the application log, which is why people miss them.

If a service logs to a file instead of the journal, the unit's StandardOutput= setting tells you where. systemctl cat is the fastest way to find out.

checks.prompt: A service died overnight with no application error in its own log. Where do you look next?
options: journalctl -k for the OOM killer or kernel events
checks.explanation: A process killed by the kernel (OOM) logs nothing itself; the evidence is in the kernel journal.

why_wrong.2: Config errors usually appear at startup, not as a silent overnight death.
why_wrong.0: DNS failures do not terminate a process.

checks.prompt: Load average is 8.0 on a 4-core machine with low CPU usage and high iowait. What is the most likely cause?
options: Processes blocked on storage IO, which also count toward load
checks.explanation: Load average includes uninterruptible (D state) tasks. High iowait with low CPU points at storage.

why_wrong.0: That would show high user CPU, not high iowait.
why_wrong.1: Memory pressure would show in swap and free memory.
why_wrong.2: DNS delays appear as socket waits, not sustained iowait.

connect.title: Sockets
connect.text: ss -ltnp links a listening port to a PID, which is how you go from 'port closed' to 'process not running'.

connect.title: Permissions
connect.text: A unit's User= setting determines which files it can read — the join with Module 6.

connect.text: The service listening mission is solved with exactly these commands.

interview.q: How do you investigate a failed systemd service?
interview.a: systemctl status for the exit code and recent lines, then journalctl -u for the full log, then systemctl cat to confirm what it actually runs and with which User/EnvironmentFile. Check the kernel log for OOM kills if the process died without logging.

interview.q: What is the difference between a process and a service?
interview.a: A process is a running program with a PID. A service is a systemd unit that manages a process or group of processes: it defines how to start and stop it, dependencies, restart policy, resource limits and where output goes.
